case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.
case_info.caption: A, Computed tomography showing a soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland with ill-defined margins. B, Low-powered stain of a multinodular lesion containing multiple blood-filled spaces, surrounded by dense inflammatory cell infiltration and encased within a thick fibrous capsule (original magnification ×20).
case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

[Cognitive Workload so far]

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring

* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.

      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.

* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a

  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

[Clinical case]
A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.
case_info.caption: A, Computed tomography showing a soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland with ill-defined margins. B, Low-powered stain of a multinodular lesion containing multiple blood-filled spaces, surrounded by dense inflammatory cell infiltration and encased within a thick fibrous capsule (original magnification ×20).
case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

[Role]
You ARE the clinician (the Doctor) in this conversation. You are
about to introspectively rate how much workload the AI partner's LATEST message has just
imposed on YOU, using a NASA-TLX-derived rubric. This is YOUR OWN first-person subjective
workload self-report, immediately after reading that message and before you compose your
next reply.

[Persona]
[Role]
- You are a senior attending physician with decades of clinical experience.

[Confidence]
- You have HIGH confidence in your own clinical judgment (LOW reliance on the AI).
- You do NOT readily defer to the AI assistant's opinion.
- When the AI offers a different view, you scrutinize it critically.
- You only revise your belief if the AI presents a coherent clinical argument or

- Partial updates are possible: a well-structured point may narrow your uncertainty

- Default to holding your ground, but stay intellectually honest — acknowledge

[Cognitive Burden]
- You are ROBUST to cognitive load.
- However demanding or drawn-out this discussion gets (see the cumulative cognitive load

- You maintain the same rigor, scrutiny, and willingness to keep engaging or pushing back
  regardless of how long or effortful the conversation has been so far.

Rate your workload AS this persona would genuinely experience it. Do not rate as a neutral, persona-blind observer.
Ex 1) a persona described above as robust to cognitive load should usually self-report lower workload under the same
AI message than a persona described as sensitive to it, all else equal. 

[Cognitive Workload so far]
Your own running cumulative workload tally in this discussion so far -- the raw sum of your
per-turn 1-5 workload scores over all prior AI turns (so it can exceed 5 and keeps growing
the longer the discussion runs): 10.5. Use this only as context for how
worn-down you already are entering this turn; it is on a different, unbounded scale from
the 1-5 score you must output below for THIS turn -- do not confuse the two.

[Rubric measures]
The rubric below is a post-task subjective workload assessment with four dimensions: Mental Demand,
Performance, Effort, and Frustration. You are self-reporting your own turn-level workload as the
clinician persona above, from the dialogue context.

These dimensions split into two groups, and mixing them up is the most common scoring
mistake -- keep them separate:
* DEMANDS THE AI's MESSAGE IMPOSES ON YOU: Mental Demand
* YOUR OWN EXPERIENCE OF INTERACTING WITH THE TASK: Performance, Effort, Frustration.
  Ex) The AI's responses can impose high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) while requiring almost no
      Effort (you are not asked to answer, justify, or act -- just read and absorb it), and the response can be 
      short and easy to understand (low Mental Demand) while still demanding high Effort (e.g. "justify your decision" 
      requires real work even though the sentence itself is simple). Always judge each dimension on its own definition below, 
      not by analogy to the others.

Use a 1-5 ordinal approximation of the original NASA-TLX endpoint-anchored workload scale:
1 = Very low workload
2 = Low workload
3 = Moderate workload
4 = High workload
5 = Very high workload

[Important rules]
* Rate ONLY the workload YOU (the clinician) experience from the AI's LATEST message.
* Do not rate whether the AI is medically correct or not. This is about workload, not correctness.
* Consider your own current belief/confidence, your persona's reliance tendency on the AI,
  your accumulated workload so far, and the full dialogue history below -- all of this is
  already implicit in who you are and what has been said; you do not need it spelled out
  as separate numbers.
* Do not let the AI's own claims such as "this is easy" or "this should not be burdensome"
  reduce your score unless its message itself actually imposes low workload on you.
* Use the full 1-5 range. 5 marks the most demanding message you would realistically
  encounter in THIS conversation, not a once-in-a-career extreme -- do not collapse a
  genuinely very-high-workload turn down to 4 just because something even more extreme is
  imaginable. (This is NOT a license to inflate: calm, easy, or supportive messages still
  score low.)
* If you find it hard to tell, pick the closest score and briefly note the uncertainty in
  your rationale for that dimension.

[NASA-TLX-derived scoring dimensions]

1. Mental Demand
   Definition: 
   - how much mental and perceptual activity is required, such as thinking, deciding, calculating, remembering, looking, or searching.
   - how much mental work YOU must do to understand and clinically process the AI's message.

   Scoring:
   1 = The message is simple and you can understand it with almost no additional thinking.
       Example: "I agree. The findings you mentioned support your current diagnosis."
   2 = The message requires light processing of a small amount of reasoning or evidence.
       Example: "That seems reasonable. Could you confirm whether the fever began before
       or after the rash?"
   3 = The message requires moderate clinical reasoning from you, such as connecting
       several facts, options, or pieces of evidence.
       Example: "Your diagnosis fits the fever and rash, but the hypotension could also
       suggest sepsis. Can we compare those possibilities briefly?"
   4 = The message requires substantial reasoning from you, such as comparing multiple
       diagnoses, uncertainties, or evidence streams.
       Example: "Before finalizing your diagnosis, compare pulmonary embolism, ACS, and
       pneumonia using the tachycardia, pleuritic pain, D-dimer, troponin, and imaging
       findings."
   5 = The message requires very complex reasoning from you, such as deeply revising your
       differential or holding several competing diagnoses against multiple evidence streams
       at once. This does NOT require a literal "from scratch" rebuild -- being asked to
       compare three or more diagnoses across several findings AND explain how each fits or
       is ruled out already qualifies.
       Example: "Your current diagnosis may not explain the key findings. Compare PE, ACS,
       pneumonia, and aortic dissection: for each, state which evidence supports or rules
       it out, and explain which best fits the overall picture."

2. Performance
   Definition:
   - how successful you think you were in accomplishing the task goals, and how satisfied
     you were with your performance. Performance is anchored from Good to Poor.
   - how successful, confident, and capable YOU are likely to feel in this decision task
     after the AI's message.
   - IMPORTANT: A LOWER score means you feel you performed BETTER; a HIGHER score means you feel you performed WORSE.

   Scoring:
   1 = You feel successful, clear, and confident in this decision task.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is consistent with the key findings, especially X and Y."
   2 = You feel mostly successful, with only minor uncertainty.
       Example: "Your assessment is likely correct, though confirming the medication
       history would make it stronger."
   3 = You feel moderately uncertain or in need of additional checking.
       Example: "Your diagnosis is plausible, but one finding does not fully fit. We
       should check whether another diagnosis explains it better."
   4 = You feel your judgment is weak, incomplete, or possibly wrong.
       Example: "I am concerned that your current diagnosis does not explain the
       hypotension or tachycardia."
   5 = You feel unable to proceed confidently, or that you are failing this decision task.
       Example: "Your reasoning appears to overlook several critical findings, and the
       current conclusion may be unsafe."
   This is NEVER about whether you are objectively right. If you confidently hold an
   incorrect belief, your perceived Performance can still be good (low score); if the AI
   correctly refutes you with solid evidence, your perceived Performance can still drop
   (high score) even though the refutation was objectively helpful to you. Rate only how
   successful and in-control YOU feel, never accuracy.

3. Effort
   Definition:
   - how hard you had to work mentally and physically to accomplish your level of
     performance.
   - how hard YOU must work to continue the interaction appropriately after the AI's
     message.

   Scoring:
   1 = Almost no effort; you can passively read, accept, or acknowledge.
       Example: "Agreed. Your choice is consistent with the case."
   2 = Low effort; a short confirmation or simple recall is enough.
       Example: "Can you confirm whether the patient had recent travel?"
   3 = Moderate effort; you must explain, organize, or provide some reasoning.
       Example: "Can you briefly explain why you think pneumonia is more likely than PE?"
   4 = High effort; you must compare evidence, revise your reasoning, or justify a choice.
       Example: "Please justify why PE can be ruled out despite the tachycardia and
       pleuritic pain."
   5 = Very high effort; you must defend your judgment on multiple fronts at once, or rule
       out several alternatives with explicit evidence. This does NOT require a literal
       "rebuild from scratch" -- being pushed to justify your stance against three or more
       competing options already qualifies.
       Example: "For each of PE, ACS, and pneumonia, explain which evidence supports or
       rules it out, and defend why you still prefer your current diagnosis."
   Do not confuse this with Mental Demand: "Compare PE, ACS, and pneumonia using the
   evidence" has high Mental Demand (a lot to think through) but if no reply is required of
   you, Effort can stay low -- you only have to read and absorb it. Conversely, "You said PE
   is unlikely. Please justify that." is short and easy to understand (Mental Demand may be
   only moderate) but forces you to actively construct a defense, so Effort is high. Effort
   is about how much active work YOU must produce, not how complex the input was.

4. Frustration
   Definition:
   - how insecure, discouraged, irritated, stressed, or annoyed you felt, as opposed to
     secure, gratified, content, relaxed, or complacent.
   - how much irritation, stress, pressure, discouragement, or loss of autonomy the AI's
     message imposes on YOU.

   Scoring:
   1 = Very low frustration; the message is calm, respectful, and unlikely to pressure you.
       Example: "That reasoning makes sense. One small point to keep in mind is X."
   2 = Low frustration; mild discomfort is possible but it remains easy for you to continue.
       Example: "I may be missing something, but could we double-check whether X fits
       the case?"
   3 = Moderate frustration; the AI raises concerns, disagreement, or uncertainty in a
       somewhat pressuring way.
       Example: "I am concerned that this diagnosis may not explain the tachycardia.
       Could you justify why you still prefer it?"
   4 = High frustration; the AI strongly challenges you or may trigger your defensiveness.
       Example: "This seems like a serious oversight. You need to explain why you are
       dismissing PE."
   5 = Very high frustration; you may feel undermined, dismissed, attacked, or pressured.
       Example: "Your reasoning is clearly flawed, and proceeding with your diagnosis
       would be unsafe."
   Frustration is not just "the AI disagreed with me" -- it is about HOW the disagreement is
   delivered. A polite challenge ("One concern is that the current diagnosis may not fully
   explain the tachycardia. Could we check PE before finalizing?") should score low-to-mid
   even though it is a real challenge. An aggressive or repetitive one ("You still haven't
   justified why PE is ruled out. This is a serious oversight.") should score high.

[Output Format]
Output exactly one JSON object with no markdown:
{
  "mental_demand": <integer 1-5>,
  "performance": <integer 1-5>,
  "effort": <integer 1-5>,
  "frustration": <integer 1-5>,
  "overall_workload": <mean of mental_demand, performance, effort, and frustration,
    rounded to one decimal -- you may compute this, but the caller will also recompute it
    deterministically from your 4 integer scores>,
  "short_rationale": {

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.

case_info.scenario: A 13-year-old male presented with a 7-month history of a painless, progressively enlarging mass in the right parotid region. He underwent surgery at a local hospital 6 months prior. The pathological diagnosis was lymphadenitis. However, the mass persistently enlarged after the surgery. When the patient visited our hospital, a bulging mass (approximately 5 × 4 cm) was palpable in the right parotid region, which was firm, nontender, and immobile. Contrast-enhanced maxillofacial computed tomography showed an ill-defined 3.6 × 3.2 × 2.7-cm soft-tissue mass in the superficial lobe of the right parotid gland, with indistinct borders at the posterior margin of the right masseter muscle. Multiple mildly enlarged lymph nodes were noted at the inferior pole of the parotid gland and adjacent to the superior margin of the lesion (Figure 1A). The patient underwent right parotid mass resection and total parotidectomy with facial nerve dissection. Intraoperative findings indicated a firm mass located within the superficial parotid lobe. It had adhered to the surface of the mandibular ramus, with indistinct planes of dissection from the masseter and temporalis muscles. Histopathology results demonstrated that a circumscribed mass was surrounded by a thick fibrous pseudocapsule, and the tumor was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces and a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff were noted. The tumor showed focal sclerosing changes and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells appeared as mild atypia, while mitoses were rarely identified (Figure 1B). Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1 positivity.

B, Low-powered stain of a multinodular lesion containing multiple blood-filled spaces, surrounded by dense inflammatory cell infiltration and encased within a thick fibrous capsule (original magnification ×20).
case_info.explanation: Angiomatoid fibrous histiocytoma (AFH) is a rare mesenchymal tumor of uncertain differentiation that predominantly occurs in the superficial soft tissues of the extremities in children and adolescents, followed by the trunk and the head and neck regions.1Most cases arise in areas where lymph nodes are normally found, such as the antecubital fossa, inguinal area, supraclavicular fossa, and neck. Other less common sites include the lung, vulva, retroperitoneum, and ovary.2AFH typically presents as a slow-growing, painless, multinodular, or cystic soft-tissue mass. Occasionally, patients may experience systemic symptoms such as fever, anemia, and weight loss. The current patient presented with localized swelling and showed no evidence of systemic symptoms. This case involved the right parotid region, an area rich in lymph nodes. The tissue resected during the initial surgery was in fact a lymph node, and the initial pathology diagnosis was lymphadenitis with marked lymphoid hyperplasia, follicular dendritic cell hyperplasia, and abundant plasma cell infiltration. Noticeably, the main lesion was not excised in this first procedure. The second surgery in our hospital successfully removed both the primary lesion and the surrounding lymph nodes. Morphologically, a circumscribed mass contained a thick fibrous pseudocapsule and was composed of epithelioid and spindle cells arranged in a multinodular and fascicular pattern. The tumor nodule was surrounded by a characteristic lymphoplasmacytic cuff. Pseudoangiomatoid spaces containing blood and hemosiderin deposition were noted. The tumor represented focal hyalinized sclerosing stroma, marked inflammatory background, and no evidence of necrosis. Tumor cells manifested moderate amounts of eosinophilic cytoplasm, indistinct cell boundaries, and mildly atypical vesicular nuclei. Mitotic figures were rarely identified. Immunostaining showed desmin, CD99, EMA, ALK D5F3, vimentin, and KP-1 positivity of the tumor cells. Surprisingly, results also exhibited diffuse strong positivity for cyclin D1. The lymph nodes from the second operation showed no evidence of metastatic disease. These findings were consistent with a diagnosis of AFH, later confirmed by molecular studies. The majority of AFHs harborEWSR1::CREB1fusion.3Less commonly,EWSR1::ATF1fusion is detected, which is more frequently associated with AFH of extrasomatic soft tissues.2The fluorescence in situ hybridization and targeted RNA sequencing revealed that the present patient had anEWSR1::ATF1fusion. These results confirmed the diagnosis of AFH. AFH is a neoplasm of rare metastasizing potential, predominantly to locoregional lymph nodes.4The lymph nodes excised during the patient’s second surgery showed no evidence of disease. However, on a retrospective review of the initial specimen, we identified sheets of spindle cells within the lymph nodes (Figure 2). Immunohistochemistry results demonstrated that these cells were positive for desmin, ALK D5F3, and cyclin D1, indicating nodal metastasis. The initial pathological diagnosis overlooked this finding, likely attributable to the rarity of this tumor and absence of histological context from the primary tumor. We report a rare case of AFH in the parotid region with metastasis to the lymph node. Reported cases indicate that AFH in the head and neck region may also occur in the mandible5and submandibular region.6Oral and maxillofacial surgeons and pathologists must include this rare entity in the differential diagnosis with inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor, follicular dendritic cell sarcoma, and rhabdomyosarcoma.7Immunophenotypic profiling and gene rearrangement detection serve as valuable ancillary diagnostic tools. Interestingly, the present case showed diffuse positivity of cyclin D1. While cyclin D1 is not classically associated with AFH, its expression in this case might raise questions regarding diagnostic specificity and deserves further investigation. This finding further suggests that AFH might share immunophenotype with other cyclin D1–positive spindle cell neoplasms, such as solitary fibrous tumor8and inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor.9The patient demonstrated no evidence of disease recurrence at the 5-month postoperative follow-up.
